title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management 2026 (AI Fact Sheet 2026)
pub: Aon — AI Fact Sheet 2026, circulated through Aon's Professional Services Practice Law Firm Advisory (Q2 2026)
author: Aon

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source does not assess whether human oversight provides effective control, independent verification, or preserves expertise. It instead reframes the issue around cross-industry exposure and predicts that court-established liability will make risks more predictable and alter behaviour.
qs: (Jury  Finds Tesla Autopilot Defective in Landmark $329  Million Verdict – What It Means for Future Cases).17  ○Copyright and other AI/PI issues will increase in  predictability once the courts establish liability –  behavior will change (even if there are a few big  verdicts/settlements).

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Aon does not directly assess whether legal AI mainly reconfigures workflows, delivers bounded productivity gains, or creates apprenticeship risks. It instead reframes operational AI risk around insurance ambiguity, explicit coverage terms and specialised products. Its emphasis on credible testing, controls and governance is consistent with the cluster’s deployment recommendations, but chiefly extends them into underwriting and risk transfer rather than substantiating the cluster’s central legal-workflow proposition.
qs: Evaluation artifacts are becoming the  lingua franca across underwriting, procurement, and oversight, and teams  that cannot produce credible evidence of testing, controls, and governance  will find decisions being made for them.
This trend suggests a move toward dedicated AI  insurance products, meaning businesses may need specialized coverage  instead of relying on CGL policies for AI-related claims.

st.t: Regulatory institutions: Governance needs implementation markets
st.an: The source supports stronger AI governance, calibrated private-sector risk management and improved agent controls, but it does not address the cluster’s central institutional proposal of publicly determined outcomes implemented through competing private regulatory markets. Its liability forecast and experimental evidence strengthen the urgency of governance without establishing a position on that market design.
qs: AI forecasters predict that up to 20% of large  enterprises will see lawsuits and fines due to  inadequate AI agent controls by 2030.22 Today’s state  of AI governance makes that a likely reality (or worse)  unless we improve AI governance immediately.

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: Aon accepts that insurance depends on policy wording and cannot substitute for governance, while materially extending the proposition with an integrated roadmap for controls, exposure mapping, loss estimation and risk transfer. It also explicitly acknowledges that immature AI claims data limit reliable loss modelling.
qs: While cyber insurance carriers have  accumulated sufficient data to build accurate cyber  loss models, we do not yet have the same amount and  quality of AI claim frequency and loss information.

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The source accepts the need to combine beneficial AI adoption with workable safeguards and materially extends the cluster through private-sector risk management, standards, and experimental evidence of a possible liability penalty for AI-enabled conduct. Its litigation forecast remains prospective, and its claim that standards define acceptable-risk thresholds is contested elsewhere in the cluster.
qs: and evolving standards, such as the National Institute of  Standards and Technology (“NIST”)   AI Risk Management Framework,19 set thresholds for  what are considered acceptable risks.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Aon accepts the need for selective, use-context-specific deployment backed by verification, testing and adaptive oversight. It materially extends the cluster by showing how underwriting requirements, insurance pricing and risk-transfer mechanisms can turn those governance principles into operational incentives and evidence demands.
qs: Superior  AI risk management means incrementally calibrating  safeguards to match AI’s maturity and impact, using  feedback signals to avoid under- or over-regulation and  governance.

Evaluation artifacts are becoming the  lingua franca across underwriting, procurement, and oversight, and teams  that cannot produce credible evidence of testing, controls, and governance  will find decisions being made for them.

kp.k: Most potential AI coverage remains silent and ambiguous
kp.d: Aon states that, as of March 2026, more than 90% of potential coverage for evolving AI perils under existing insurance policies is “Silent AI”: policies neither affirmatively cover nor exclude AI. It analogizes this ambiguity to early “Silent Cyber” coverage and argues that lessons from cyber insurance could accelerate clarification through affirmative grants, exclusions and standalone AI products.
qs: As a result, to the extent that evolving AI perils might be covered by existing insurance policies, such coverage falls over ninety percent (90%) under “Silent AI” insurance.
Silent AI coverage means that the underlying policy neither affirmatively covers AI nor excludes AI – the policies don’t mention AI.
If we leverage the lessons learned from cyber, we can expedite the AI risk management improvement curve.

kp.k: Insurance can shape AI governance and standards
kp.d: The document argues that insurance does more than compensate losses: underwriting can reward controls, clarify standards of care, validate operational practices and translate risk into pricing. Aon presents insurance as a dynamic signal of the expected frequency and severity of AI perils, while acknowledging that AI claims data are not yet as mature as cyber-loss data.
qs: Insurance does more than transfer risk after the fact; it rewards stronger risk controls, clarifies standards of care, validates operational discipline and translates risk into transparent price signals.
While cyber insurance carriers have accumulated sufficient data to build accurate cyber loss models, we do not yet have the same amount and quality of AI claim frequency and loss information.
Insurance can act like a real time, dynamic and fluid “prediction market”2 regarding the frequency and severity of AI perils as legacy and new policies clarify the scope of AI coverage and premium.

kp.k: Aon recommends an eight-step AI risk roadmap
kp.d: Aon recommends cataloguing organizational AI use, building a risk register, mapping perils to existing policies, identifying coverage gaps, quantifying frequency and severity, implementing governance controls, calculating total cost of risk and selecting insurance or alternative risk transfer. Its proposed controls include board oversight, contractual liability allocation, training, evaluations, third-party assessments, technical safeguards, monitoring and incident response.
qs: 1-Engage appropriate stakeholders to identify and catalogue all AI use of organization
2-Build AI risk register of related AI risks based on organization’s AI use

6-Mitigate AI risks via risk management governance best practices, which combines board oversight, contractual allocation of liability, internal training, legal/regulatory/IP engagement, evaluations/third party assessments/certifications, technical safeguards (including IT security), monitoring, and incident response
8-Implement AI insurance/alternative risk transfer program consistent with organization’s enterprise risk management, priorities, objectives and key performance indicators

kp.k: Enterprise AI adoption and spending are rapidly increasing
kp.d: Citing the 2026 AON Ponemon Intangible Risk Comparison Report and other external sources, Aon reports that 86% of respondents use or plan to use AI within 12 months. It also reports average enterprise AI spending of $7 million per organization in 2025, up 180% from $2.5 million in 2024, with a projection of $11.6 million for 2026; these are reported figures and forecasts rather than findings independently established in the fact sheet.
qs: Most organizations (86 percent of respondents) use or intend to use artificial intelligence (AI)products or services.
Average enterprise AI spending per organization hit $7 million in 2025, a 180% jump from $2.5 million in 2024, with projections of $11.6 million for 2026.
Hyperscalers are planning to pour $1.3 trillion into AI infrastructure through 2027.

kp.k: AI adoption is affecting promotion and professional-services pricing
kp.d: The document reports cross-domain evidence from consulting and auditing that AI use is being incorporated into employee advancement and client pricing. It says an unnamed global consulting firm links AI-tool use to promotion and may exit non-adopters, while KPMG reportedly obtained a 14% audit-fee reduction from Grant Thornton after demanding that AI savings be passed through. Aon frames such examples as part of a debate over whether AI efficiency gains should reduce professional-services fees.
qs: In order to position itself as a leader in artificial intelligence, a world-wide leading consulting firm is linking use of AI tools to promotion potential and will exit employees who are not adopting the use of AI at work.
KPMG threatened to find a new auditor if Grant Thornton did not pass on savings from AI, leading to a 14% reduction in the audit fee, dropping from $416,000 in 2024 to $357,000 in 2025.

This, and similar cases, highlight a growing debate in professional services where clients demand that efficiency gains from AI (speeding up document triage, risk assessment, etc.) should be reflected in lower fees.

kp.k: Demand for explicit AI insurance is substantial
kp.d: Drawing on external market research, Aon reports that more than 90% of organizations see a need for AI- or generative-AI-specific coverage and that over two-thirds would pay at least 10% more for explicit extensions. It also relays a forecast that standalone AI insurance will reach $4.8 billion annually by 2032.
qs: The standalone artificial intelligence insurance market is expected to become a $4.8 billion annual market by 2032.
More than 90% of organizations see a need for insurance coverage tailored to AI/Generative AI threats.
Over two thirds would pay at least 10% more in premiums for explicit insurance policy extensions that cover Gen/AI related risks.

kp.k: Professional liability maps to most observed AI claims
kp.d: Based on Aon’s directional aggregation of more than 250 AI-related cases as of December 2025, the document estimates that approximately 80% of current claims may be addressed by errors and omissions, professional liability or media liability insurance. It says customized “all-risk” E&O addresses about 80% versus approximately 58% for typical named-risk E&O, while fewer than 10% of organizations buy E&O. Categories overlap, so the percentages are not additive and do not establish that coverage applies in any particular case.
qs: Aon aggregated AI-related claims data from multiple sources (250+ cases as of December 2025).

Approximately 80% of current AI claims can be addressed by Errors & Omissions/Professional Liability/Media Liability Insurance – a lot of copyright infringement and Advertising Injury and Personal Injury claims to date, but less than 10% of organizations purchase E & O (typical “named risk” risk E & O policies cover approximately 58% of AI claims compared to 80% addressed by customized “all-risk” E & O).
there can be overlap and gaps so the following does not add up to 100%

kp.k: Cyber and other policies address smaller overlapping shares
kp.d: The same Aon case-mapping exercise estimates that standalone cyber insurance may address approximately 15% of current AI claims and other lines approximately 20%, including D&O for “AI washing,” employment practices liability for employment discrimination and crime coverage for deepfake funds-transfer fraud. These are directional mappings to potentially responsive insuring agreements, not determinations of actual coverage.
qs: Approximately 15% of current AI claims can be addressed by standalone cyber insurance.

Approximately 20% of current claims can be addressed by other lines of insurance, such as Director’s & Officer’s (“AI washing”); Employment Practices Liability Insurance (employment related discrimination); Crime (deepfake financial fraud/ funds transfer); General Liability; Intellectual Property; Property; etc.
Output provides directional analysis to understand which insuring agreements may address these types of lawsuits

kp.k: Legal hallucinations create professional-services liability exposure
kp.d: In its industry risk taxonomy, Aon identifies hallucinated legal analysis, disclosure of confidential client data, intellectual-property exposure and automated analytical errors as AI perils for professional and business services. The document uses “hallucinations” to mean erroneous or fabricated AI output rather than court-sanctions incidents specifically.
qs: AI hallucinations in research, legal analysis, or advisory
Unintentional exposure of confidential client data
Intellectual property risks
Automated financial or analytical model errors

kp.k: AI-assisted errors may worsen access-to-justice problems
kp.d: An endnote characterizes first-quarter 2026 developments as showing that courts increasingly treat AI-assisted errors not only as a lawyer issue but also as an access-to-justice issue. It argues that testing, controls and governance evidence are becoming important across underwriting, procurement and oversight, although the fact sheet does not provide the underlying court decisions or empirical details in its main text.
qs: At the same time, courts are now explicitly signaling that AI-assisted errors are not just a lawyer problem, they are an access-to-justice problem, and hiring tech is facing a new round of legal scrutiny over opaque scoring.

Evaluation artifacts are becoming the lingua franca across underwriting, procurement, and oversight, and teams that cannot produce credible evidence of testing, controls, and governance will find decisions being made for them.

kp.k: Underwriters increasingly examine human verification and auditability
kp.d: The representative insurance application questions show carriers focusing on whether a human verifies AI output before action, whether actions are logged for review and remediation, and how organizations prevent bias. These questions make human verification, traceability and governance relevant to insurability, but the document does not claim that any single control guarantees coverage.
qs: Does a human need to verify accuracy before AI takes action?
Are AI actions logged so potential errors can be reviewed and remediated?
How do you prevent unintended bias when utilizing AI?
Do you have an AI Governance Framework with Board/Management oversight, which includes specific use cases, restrictions and authorization policies?

kp.k: AI contracting requires explicit rights and liability allocation
kp.d: Aon recommends diligence into vendors’ AI use and safeguards, along with contractual clarity over ownership and permitted use of prompts and outputs, confidentiality, indemnities, hold-harmless provisions, service levels, plugins and APIs. It also highlights insurance-backed intellectual-property indemnities and representations that providers comply with applicable law.
qs: Are you confirming whether any key vendors are utilizing AI, and if so, what safeguards are in place to prevent errors or bias? Have you conducted pre-contract diligence?
Who owns and has what rights to use the prompts (inputs) and outputs?
What is the allocation of liability, including hold harmless and indemnity?
If yes, please confirm whether indemnities are provided in respect of IP infringement by the licensor, and whether such indemnities carry insurance backing.

kp.k: AI exclusions are proliferating across legacy policies
kp.d: Aon warns that organizations must map AI risks to policies as exclusions and sublimits proliferate. It reports optional ISO endorsements excluding generative-AI exposures from commercial general liability policies and examples of broader insurer exclusions, suggesting a movement toward dedicated AI products. Actual outcomes remain dependent on policy wording, allegations, insured status and other case-specific facts.
qs: Map Your Organization’s AI Risks to Existing Insurance as AI Exclusions and sub-limit provisions proliferate

Insurance Services Office (ISO), a Verisk business and major provider of standard policy forms, introduced new optional endorsements to exclude Generative Artificial Intelligence exposures from Commercial General Liability policies.
This trend suggests a move toward dedicated AI insurance products, meaning businesses may need specialized coverage instead of relying on CGL policies for AI-related claims.
More broadly insurance policies vary, often significantly, in terms of coverage terms and conditions, including exclusions.

kp.k: AI users may face an experimental liability penalty
kp.d: Aon reports a forthcoming Stanford Journal of Law, Economics & Business article suggesting that factfinders may treat AI-enabled conduct more harshly. In an experiment inspired by automated-bot scraping litigation, participants were reportedly more inclined to impose liability and higher damages when defendants used AI. The fact sheet presents this as preliminary experimental research, not established case law.
qs: Case law on these questions in the context of AI is developing, but a forthcoming article in the Stanford Journal of Law, Economics & Business suggests juries may treat AI-enabled conduct more harshly in legal disputes, resulting in what the authors call an “AI penalty.”
In an experiment inspired by a case involving automated-bot scraping, the authors found that factfinders may be more inclined to find liability and award higher damages when defendants use AI.

kp.k: Inadequate agent controls may generate lawsuits and fines
kp.d: The document relays a forecast that up to 20% of large enterprises will face lawsuits and fines from inadequate AI-agent controls by 2030. Aon endorses the concern by arguing that present governance makes that result likely or worse unless governance improves immediately, but the numerical projection is attributed to external forecasters rather than Aon’s own measured claims data.
qs: AI forecasters predict that up to 20% of large enterprises will see lawsuits and fines due to inadequate AI agent controls by 2030.
Today’s state of AI governance makes that a likely reality (or worse) unless we improve AI governance immediately.

kp.k: Risk quantification should drive governance and capital decisions
kp.d: Aon recommends model inventories, scenario modelling, end-to-end audits, vendor diligence, bias testing, contractual indemnities and dedicated governance leads. It proposes mapping event frequency and severity by sector and insurance line, then using actuarial analysis to choose retention, insurance or alternative risk transfer; captives or catastrophe bonds may be needed for aggregated, correlated or systemic risks.
qs: Through these lenses, organizations can implement a range of best practices, including maintaining an AI model inventory, quantifying exposures through scenario modeling, conducting end-to-end AI system audits, performing third-party vendor due diligence, implementing unacceptable bias detection and validation testing, defining contractual indemnities, and appointing dedicated governance leads for AI deployment.
These practices help translate risk into measurable risk mitigation action.
For potential aggregated, correlated, systemic risks, insureds may need to consider alternative risk transfer, such as a captive or catastrophe bonds.

kp.k: Governance intensity should match application risk
kp.d: Aon advocates iterative, proportionate governance rather than uniform controls: healthcare, defense and autonomous systems should receive stricter oversight than marketing automation. It recommends piloting frameworks and adjusting them using adoption, incident, trust and compliance-cost indicators, while characterizing stable incidents alongside rising adoption as evidence of balance and flat adoption with rising costs as possible over-scrutiny.
qs: We can scale incremental guardrails to the maturity and criticality of AI applications.
For example, higher-risk AI like healthcare, defense, and autonomous robotics, such as drones and vehicles should face stricter oversight than low-risk AI like marketing automation.
By deploying an iterative risk calibration, insurance underwriters, regulators and organizations can pilot-test AI risk frameworks, observe impacts, and then adjust AI governance in phases.
For example, a rise in AI adoption rates alongside stable risk incidents suggests governance is well-balanced. Conversely, flat AI adoption with rising compliance costs signals over-scrutiny.

kp.k: Better governance is predicted to improve insurability
kp.d: The document predicts a feedback loop in which effective controls reduce risk, leading insurers to broaden coverage and adjust premiums, which in turn supports innovation and protection. This is Aon’s proposed mechanism and strategic argument, not an empirical finding demonstrated with comparative premium or loss data in the document.
qs: If an AI safety implementation is effective at reducing AI risk, then insurers will broaden insurance coverage robustness and adjust premium rates accordingly.
This creates a virtuous cycle: good governance leads to better insurability, which in turn supports innovation and insureds’ protection.
Better access to AI insurance markets translates to lower premiums, which frees up capital for research & development and scaling.

kp.k: Long-term AI outcomes remain highly disputed and speculative
kp.d: Aon summarizes sharply conflicting expert scenarios, from extinction caused by superintelligence to major gains in healthcare, education, science and productivity. It attributes catastrophic claims to sources including “AI 2027,” Geoffrey Hinton, Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares, while noting that Yann LeCun considers existential catastrophe effectively impossible. The document treats these as uncertain scenarios requiring quantification, not settled predictions.
qs: A white paper titled: “AI 2027”28 posits a range of scenarios involving AI systems surpassing human-level intelligence, and actions by policymakers could determine whether the consequences are catastrophic.

Geoffrey Hinton, the widely considered “Godfather of AI,” sees two main future possibilities for the relationship between humans and AI’s: either AI’s take over and humanity goes extinct, or AI amplifies human potential and greatly improves healthcare, education, scientific discovery, productivity, and the economy; it democratizes knowledge, helps address climate change, and enhances standards of living.
However, the probability of doom (i.e., the probability of catastrophic, human-extinction-level outcomes caused by advanced AGI) referred to by AI computer scientists as p(doom), is not preordained.
Yann LeCun, a prominent AI researcher and Chief AI Scientist at Meta, believes the probability of an AI-caused existential catastrophe is effectively zero.

kp.k: Coverage conclusions remain policy-specific and qualified
kp.d: Aon repeatedly qualifies its coverage analysis: policy grids and claim mappings are general information, do not modify actual terms and cannot establish that a particular loss is insured. Coverage depends on the policy type, wording, exclusions, allegations and facts, and Aon directs readers to legal, financial and insurance advisers.
qs: All descriptions, summaries or highlights of coverage described herein are for general informational purposes only and do not amend, alter or modify the actual terms and conditions of any relevant policy.
Coverage is governed only by the terms and conditions of such policy.
Insurance coverage in any particular case will depend upon the type of policy in effect, the terms, conditions and exclusions in any such policy, and the facts of each unique situation.
No representation is made that any specific insurance coverage would apply in the circumstances outlined herein.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Aon argues that AI creates growing, changing liability exposures and insurance demand, while governance and explicit coverage can support adoption. Its principal claims concern insurance and professional-services risk rather than the replacement of lawyers.
pts.d: Aon says AI development has outpaced risk management and that over 90% of potentially available existing coverage is silent about AI. It anticipates a shift toward explicit coverage and exclusions, analogous to cyber insurance. Its litigation mapping suggests professional liability/E&O/media liability may address approximately 80% of current AI claims, versus approximately 15% for cyber and 20% for other lines, with overlap. Aon predicts bodily injury and tangible property damage claims will grow materially as robotics, autonomous vehicles and other physical deployments expand, while copyright disputes should become more predictable as courts establish liability. For professional and business services, it identifies hallucinations in legal analysis, confidential-client-data exposure, IP risks and analytical errors. It reports pressure on professional-services providers to pass AI efficiencies to clients, using an audit-fee reduction as its example, not a law-firm pricing study. It presents a forecast that inadequate agent controls could expose up to 20% of large enterprises to lawsuits and fines by 2030 and endorses that outcome as likely absent improved governance. It also reports an experimental finding of an 'AI penalty' in liability judgments. Aon argues that effective safeguards can improve insurability, coverage and premiums, freeing capital for innovation; it separately presents potential insurance-industry cost and premium reductions from AI productivity as theoretical. It reports a forecast of a $4.8 billion annual standalone AI insurance market by 2032 and predicts AI will remain a defining megatrend for at least a decade.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines Aon's directional litigation mapping and insurance-practitioner experience with surveys, reported cases, external forecasts and an experiment; these are not all findings of observed AI losses or confirmed coverage.
pts.d: Aon aggregated more than 250 AI-related cases as of December 2025 from multiple sources, including the GW DAIL and Stanford class-action databases, and mapped allegations to insurance lines. The endnote explicitly describes this as directional analysis of which insuring agreements may address lawsuits, not claims-payment evidence. Aon acknowledges insufficient AI claim-frequency and loss data relative to cyber and promotes its diagnostic tool as a response. The silent-coverage estimate is dated March 2026 without a calculation method. Survey evidence includes the Aon/Ponemon report's 86% using or intending to use AI and Geneva Association findings that more than 90% want tailored coverage and over two-thirds would pay at least 10% more for explicit extensions. The 2032 market projection is attributed in the endnotes to Deloitte; the agent-control forecast to IDC. The fee-pressure example is a reported KPMG demand that its auditor Grant Thornton share AI savings, resulting in a reported 14% fee reduction from $416,000 in 2024 to $357,000 in 2025. This is an audit-client example, not evidence of Big Four entry into legal services. Physical-risk examples include a reported Tesla Autopilot verdict and a technician's alleged robot injury lawsuit. The 'AI penalty' claim is based on an experiment inspired by automated-bot scraping, discussed in a forthcoming journal article, rather than a general measurement of court outcomes. Aon's governance-to-insurability argument rests on practitioner reasoning and historical analogy; its references to catastrophic AI and rapid labor-market disruption are attributed external scenarios and views, not its own measured forecasts.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source distinguishes present coverage ambiguity from near-term changes in claims and longer-term market forecasts, and makes coverage and premium outcomes conditional.
pts.d: The litigation analysis uses cases through December 2025; the silent-AI estimate is as of March 2026. The predicted shift toward physical injury and property damage is framed as occurring within the next few years and depends on expanded physical AI deployment. Greater copyright predictability depends on courts establishing liability and subsequent behavioral change. The agent-control forecast runs to 2030, the standalone insurance-market forecast to 2032, and the megatrend prediction covers at least the next decade. Reduced insurance costs and premiums depend on AI actually increasing accuracy, efficiency and productivity, all else equal. Improved coverage and pricing depend on safeguards demonstrably reducing risk, while governance must be continually recalibrated to application maturity and criticality. Aon repeatedly qualifies coverage as dependent on policy wording, exclusions, claim allegations and the insured; its mapping is not a coverage guarantee. The extracted coverage grid has lost its color coding, so individual cells cannot reliably establish affirmative, silent, ambiguous or excluded coverage. Document dating is internally mixed: the supplied heading describes April/Q2 2026 circulation, while the closing page says publication as of August 1, 2026.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include AI deployers and providers, professional-services firms and clients, insurers and brokers, corporate governance teams, and people harmed by AI-enabled decisions or physical systems.
pts.d: Law firms receive the document as risk-management guidance: AI-assisted legal analysis and confidential client information create professional-liability and information risks, while exclusions can alter available protection. Aon does not quantify lawyer displacement, staffing changes or legal-market shares. Professional-services clients are portrayed as demanding lower fees when AI produces efficiencies; providers face corresponding pricing pressure. AI providers and deployers face questions about contractual liability, IP rights, disclosures, vendor diligence and human verification before AI acts. Boards, managers, risk teams and procurement functions are expected to inventory uses, document controls and demonstrate governance to insurers. Insurers and brokers face uncertain loss models, coverage disputes, new underwriting requirements and opportunities for tailored products; buyers may need bespoke coverage or alternative risk transfer for systemic exposures. Individuals may experience discrimination, privacy breaches, fraud or physical injury. An endnote characterizes AI-assisted errors as an access-to-justice issue, but offers no identified court decision or quantified justice-gap impact in the supplied text.
